chunks: Sa'd ibn Abdillah narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Najran and al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Hariz ibn Abdillah, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who acts as imam and begins with the praise [Al-Fatihah] but does not recite 'In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful'. He said: 'It does not harm him, and there is no objection to it.' This is attributed to the state of taqiyya (dissimulation), because in taqiyya it is permissible to conceal it. It is also possible that he (peace be upon him) meant one who does not recite it out of forgetfulness, because whoever forgets it is not harmed and it is not obligatory upon him to repeat the prayer. We will clarify this later. And that which indicates that in the state of taqiyya it is permissible not to proclaim it is what has been narrated:

key_terms.بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَنِ الرَّحِيمِ: Bismillah (In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful)

ai.seo_question: Does omitting 'Bismillah' at the start of prayer invalidate the Salat according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi records this ruling from Imam al-Sadiq (AS), clarifying that omitting the Basmala is excusable either due to taqiyya (where silence is permissible) or simple forgetfulness (which does not require prayer repetition). This distinction highlights the Shia jurisprudential nuance between intentional concealment and unintentional omission in the validity of Salah. The hadith serves as a foundational text for understanding the flexibility in recitation requirements during congregational prayer.
